title: The Baseline

pages.text:
*The Surveyor's Catechism, Seventh Saying: Everything is built on one line. Get the line right.*

The Salt Flat did not have a horizon so much as an ending. It was a white void, seamless and terrifyingly empty, stretching out in every direction until the sky and the earth merged into a single, pale grey smear. Isla stood in the center of it, her boots sinking slightly into the crusted surface, and felt small in a way that had nothing to do with height and everything to do with scale.

"Stop staring," Vasht said. He was adjusting the leg of his tripod, his grey coat heavy with dust, and he did not look up. "Staring is for tourists. We are here to make a line. A line is the only thing that matters here. Everything else is a calculation."

"A calculation," Mags repeated, tying the laces of her red canvas shoes with the focused intensity of a surgeon. "So we’re measuring the flat."

"We are measuring the truth of the flat," Vasht corrected. "The baseline is the spine of the survey. If it is wrong, everything built upon it is a lie. If it is right, it becomes the standard by which we judge every other distance in the Unmade. It must be measured with a precision that makes the devil weep."

Joss was already unpacking the equipment. He moved with the brisk, purposeful energy of a man who preferred building things to explaining them. He pulled a coil of steel chain from the wagon, the links clinking softly in the thin air. "Spring balance," he said, holding up a brass device with a coiled spring inside. "Holds the tension constant. No matter how hard you pull, the spring gives, and the weight stays the same. That’s how we stop the chain from sagging."

Isla watched him set the frame up. It was a simple tripod, but the mechanism at the top was elegant. A hook, a spring, a weight. "It’s like a brake on a wagon," she said. "You apply pressure, and it releases exactly enough to keep the wheel turning smoothly."

Joss grinned, a quick, crinkling expression. "Exactly. Except the wheel is the ground, and we’re trying to make sure it doesn’t move."

Vasht pointed to the first peg, a sharp steel spike driven into the salt. "Mark the zero. Then we go. One hundred links at a time. No shortcuts. No estimates. We are here to be scrupulous."

Isla took the field-book from her coat pocket. The paper was crisp, the lines ruled in pale blue ink. She uncapped her pen. "Zero," she said, writing the time and the temperature. "Ready."

The wind picked up, whispering across the flat. It sounded like dry parchment sliding over a drafting table. Isla steadied her hand, feeling the salt crystals crunch under her boots, and waited for the first link to be pulled taut.
pages.image: A vast white salt flat under a pale grey sky; Isla in a mustard-yellow coat and dark-green trousers stands holding a field-book, while Joss in a rust-red shirt sets up a brass spring-balance tripod on a steel peg, Mags in a teal jacket ties her red shoes, and Master Vasht in a grey coat adjusts a tripod leg.

pages.text:
The rhythm of the work settled into a mechanical pulse that beat through the thin, cold air, a steady drumbeat of *pull, stretch, mark*. The chain sang a high, thin note as it was drawn taut, a sound like a bow drawn across a string, while Isla counted the links, her eyes scanning the steel, her pen scratching on the page. One, two, three... fifty. The number felt heavy in her mouth.

"Chain!" Joss called, his voice crisp and cutting through the wind.

Mags, who had been carrying the chain over her shoulder, adjusted her grip. Her deep-brown skin was flushed with the cold, her short black twists tied back with a bright blue scarf that snapped in the breeze. "Coming," she said. She walked the chain forward, her red shoes crunching on the salt crust.

Isla watched the chain stretch out, a straight line of steel against the white ground. She recorded the reading. "Mark!" she called.

Joss drove the peg into the salt with a sharp, decisive thump. *Thud.* The sound echoed faintly, then died. "Tally!"

Isla wrote the number. Her hand was steady, though her fingers were numb inside her gloves. The sun was low, casting long, distorted shadows across the flat. The glare was intense, a white fire that made her eyes water. She squinted, blinking rapidly to keep the tears from blurring her vision.

"Break time?" Mags asked, leaning on the chain. Her breath came out in small, white clouds.

"No," Vasht said. He was walking ahead, his walking stick tapping the ground. "We have most of a mile to go. And the sun is not done with us."

Joss wiped his brow with the back of his hand. "I like the sun," he said, with a grin that was more exhaustion than joy. "It’s warm."

"It’s a furnace," Isla said. "And we are the coal."

Mags laughed, a short, sharp sound. "I prefer the furnace. At least it’s honest."

They kept moving. The chain stretched, the pegs went in, the numbers were written. The landscape did not change. It was a white void, endless and indifferent. But the line grew, a thin thread of steel connecting the known to the unknown. Isla felt a strange sense of satisfaction in the repetition. It was not exciting, but it was solid. It was real.

"Another hundred," Joss said, his voice slightly hoarse.

Isla nodded. "Ready."

The wind picked up again, swirling dust around their boots. Isla tightened her grip on the pen. The line was holding.
pages.image: A wide shot of the salt flat with a long, straight steel chain stretched taut between two wooden pegs; Isla in a mustard coat crouches to write in a field-book, Joss in a rust-red shirt pulls the chain, Mags in a teal jacket carries a coil of chain, and Vasht in a grey coat walks ahead with a walking stick.

pages.text:
The noon heat had altered the terms of the engagement. The salt, which had been crisp and cold under their boots until an hour ago, now radiated a dry, intense warmth that seemed to rise from the ground and seep directly into their bones. The air shimmered above the white crust, creating a heat haze that made the distant pegs wobble with the precarious instability of a candle flame in a draft.

Vasht stopped. He held up a hand, and the chain slackened against the ground with a dull, metallic sigh. "Thermometer," he said, his voice flat and commanding.

Isla pulled the small brass instrument from her coat pocket. The mercury column rose, trembling slightly before it stopped. She read the number. "Thirty-two degrees."

"Record it," Vasht said. "And apply the correction."

Isla frowned, tapping the pen against her thigh. "The chain is steel. It expands when it is hot. That means it is longer than it should be. If we do not correct for it, we will be measuring too short."

"Precisely," Vasht said. "A careless number is a lie. And a lie, in this field, bends the land. We do not want to bend the land. We want to hold it."

Mags, who had been sitting on a rock, looked up, her blue scarf bright against the pale dust. "So we add a little?"

"Add," Isla said. "A hot chain is longer than its marks say, so each pull covers more ground than we credit it. The expansion is small, but it is there. We have to account for it."

She did the calculation in her head, the numbers dancing in the heat. It was a simple formula, but it required care. She wrote the correction down, then added it to the reading. The numbers settled into place, neat and orderly.

Mags leaned over her shoulder. "That is a lot of work," she said.

"It is a lot of care," Isla said. "And it is the only way to be sure."

Mags nodded slowly. She looked at the chain, then at the sky. "I like it," she said. "It is like adding a secret ingredient to a recipe. You cannot see it, but you can taste it."

Isla smiled, despite the fatigue. "Something like that."

They moved on. The chain stretched, the pegs went in, and the numbers were written. The heat pressed down on them, heavy and relentless. But the line held. And with every stretch, the flat became a little less empty, a little more defined.

Isla wrote the final number for the half-mile. She checked it twice. Then she looked up at Mags, who was watching her with a bright, curious expression.

"Did you get it right?" Mags asked.

Isla hesitated. "I think so. But we will check again tomorrow."

Mags grinned. "Good. I like checking. It is the only part of the job that makes me feel smart."
pages.image: Close up of Isla’s ink-stained fingers writing in a field-book held by Mags, who has deep-brown skin and a blue scarf; a brass thermometer lies on the white salt crust, the mercury column visible, under a bright, hazy sun that shimmers over the distant white horizon.

pages.text:
Dusk settled over the Salt Flat, draining the white light from the sky until the world turned a deep, bruised violet. The shadows stretched long and thin, giving the flat a sudden, startling depth it had not possessed in the noon glare. The surveyor’s pegs rose from the salt crust like the dark, iron pins of a compass rose.

Vasht stood at the end of the line, his hat pulled low over his eyes. He looked tired, but his voice remained steady, anchored like the plumb bob he carried. "We are done for today."

Joss dropped to his knees on the salt, letting out a groan that sounded like a rusted hinge working. "Finally," he said. "I thought I was going to melt."

"You didn’t melt," Mags said, pouring water from a flask into a cup. "You just got warm."

"I prefer 'warm' to 'melted,'" Joss said, taking the cup with a relieved shudder. "It sounds less fatal."

Vasht sat down on a flat rock, his walking stick resting across his knees. He looked at the line, then at Isla. "Tomorrow, we do it again."

Joss choked on his water. "What?"

"In the opposite direction," Vasht said. "From the other end. Same precision. Same care."

Isla felt a sharp spike of fatigue, but something else, a bright, humming anticipation, sat right beneath it. "Why?" she asked.

"Because one measurement is a guess," Vasht said. "Two honest measurements that agree are a fact. We need the fact, Isla. Not the guess."

Mags nodded, her eyes bright with the light of understanding. "Redundancy," she said. "It’s like having two keys to the same door. If one is broken, you still get in."

"Exactly," Vasht said. He looked at the line, then at the sky. "We are not done. We are just getting started."

Isla looked at the line, the thin, straight thread of steel that stretched into the distance. It was a small thing, a fragile thing. But it was also a promise. A promise that they could make sense of the chaos, that they could bring order to the void.

She felt a strange sense of pride, a quiet, steady warmth in her chest. It was not the thrill of discovery, but the satisfaction of work well done.

"Tomorrow, then," she said.

Vasht nodded. "Tomorrow."

The stars began to appear, one by one, like pins pushed into a black felt board. The flat was silent, except for the wind, which whispered across the salt.
pages.image: The salt flat at dusk with a purple sky and emerging stars; Vasht in a grey coat sits on a rock looking at the long straight line of pegs, Joss in a rust-red shirt kneels drinking from a cup, Mags in a teal jacket stands holding a water flask, and Isla in a mustard coat looks at the line with a thoughtful expression.

pages.text:
The second measurement was a test of patience. The sun hung low, casting a soft, amber light that made the salt flat shimmer, and the chain felt lighter in their hands, its links clicking softly against the crust. They worked in a shared silence, the rhythm of pull, stretch, mark settling into a kind of meditation. The numbers came easily, almost too easily, flowing onto the page with a deceptive smoothness.

When they finished, Vasht gathered them around the field desk. He took the book, his thick forefinger running down the columns of figures with the slow, deliberate care of a man reading a legal contract. His face remained unreadable, a mask of absolute concentration.

"Compare," he said.

Isla and Mags exchanged a glance, then both looked at the numbers, the two sets of readings lying side by side in the margin. The difference was small, barely a fraction of a link, a discrepancy so slight it might have been a trick of the eye.

"Two fingers," Mags said, pointing at the gap. "Over a mile. That’s... that’s good."

"It’s not good enough," Vasht said. "It’s close. But it’s not perfect. And in this field, close is not the same as right."

Joss frowned, scratching at his freckled cheek. "But it’s the same line. We measured it the same way. Why is it different?"

"Because something is wrong," Vasht said. "And we need to find it. We need to show our work."

Isla looked at the numbers, her mind racing through the corrections, the temperature adjustments, the tension readings. Everything seemed right on paper. And yet.

"There," she said, pointing to a small discrepancy in the middle of the line. "Here. The third peg. The reading is slightly off."

Vasht nodded. "Go and look."

They walked to the third peg, which was driven into the salt just like the others. But as Isla knelt and looked closely at the base, she saw it. A thin layer of salt crust, a white flake that had settled over the peg head. It was barely visible, a speck of white on white.

"It’s a salt crust," she said. "It’s making the peg sit higher than it should. The chain is hitting the crust, not the peg."

Mags grinned, a wide, relieved expression. "That’s it. That’s the error. A speck of salt."

Vasht smiled, a small, faint smile. "Now you have a baseline. Not before."

Isla looked at the peg, then at the line stretching out into the distance. It was a small thing, a tiny flaw in the record. But it was the flaw that mattered, the one they had to own. She reached out and brushed the salt crust away. The peg was clean, solid, true.

"Now," Vasht said, "we have a line. And a line is the beginning of everything."
pages.image: A close-up of a steel peg in white salt with a small white salt crust at its base; Isla’s hand in a mustard-yellow sleeve reaches out to brush the crust away, while Mags in a teal jacket looks on with a grin and Vasht in a grey coat watches with a faint smile.

words: showing great care and accuracy in doing something
the state of being stretched tight
the quality of having more than what is needed
a difference or inconsistency between things
not securely in place; dangerously unstable
